title: The Taming of the Shrew
author: William Shakespeare
openingChapterLabel: Act 1, Scene 1 — Padua. A public place
about:
Baptista, a rich Paduan gentleman, has two daughters: the sharp-tongued Katherina, whom no one will marry, and her younger sister Bianca, whom every young man in the city wants. Baptista refuses to let Bianca marry until Katherina is wed. Petruchio, a young gentleman of Verona, arrives in Padua looking for a rich wife. He hears about Katherina, takes the dare, and marries her within a few scenes. The rest of the main plot is Petruchio's campaign to 'tame' her — depriving her of food, sleep, and a wedding feast — until she agrees with everything he says.

While this is happening, two suitors compete for Bianca: the young Lucentio, who disguises himself as a Latin tutor to get into the house, and the elderly Gremio. Lucentio wins. The play ends at a triple wedding banquet at which the three husbands bet on whose wife is most obedient. Katherina delivers, on cue, a speech about a wife's duty to her husband that has been argued about ever since.

Shakespeare wrote The Taming of the Shrew very early, probably around 1592, while still in his late twenties. It is his most uncomfortable comedy: a Restoration revision tried to soften it; the Victorians cut it; modern productions argue over whether the final speech is sincere, ironic, or coerced. It is also one of his most successful, the basis of Cole Porter's Kiss Me, Kate, the film 10 Things I Hate About You, and a steady stream of modern productions that keep finding new ways to read it.

angleCards.title: The Katherina problem.
angleCards.text: The play's central question is what to make of Katherina's transformation. Is she broken, persuaded, in love, performing, or all of these? The final speech is the place to settle the question.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to track Katherina's arc from her first appearance to her last speech, and decide for myself whether the play 'tames' her, whether she is in earnest at the end, or whether something else is going on.

angleCards.title: Petruchio's methods.
angleCards.text: Petruchio uses sleep deprivation, food deprivation, and the trick of agreeing with everything Katherina says while denying her what she wants. The play calls this 'taming'; we have other names for it now.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Petruchio's 'taming' campaign with attention to what he actually does to Katherina — and to whether the play endorses, mocks, or simply records it.

angleCards.title: The Bianca plot.
angleCards.text: The other plot is a classic comedy of disguises: tutors who are really suitors, suitors swapping identities, fathers being deceived. It is the polite, conventional courtship that Petruchio and Katherina's marriage upends.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Bianca plot beside the Katherina plot to see what the play thinks of polite courtship — and which sister, by the end, has the better marriage.

angleCards.title: The frame and the question of irony.
angleCards.text: The play starts with a frame: a drunk tinker is tricked into watching a play performed for him. Shakespeare leaves the frame unfinished. The question of whether the whole 'taming' is a play-within-a-play that we are not meant to take straight has bothered critics for four centuries.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to attend to the play's opening frame — the trick on Christopher Sly — and decide whether it changes how the main plot should be read.

cast.name: Katherina
cast.description: Baptista's elder daughter, fierce, articulate, and refusing to be put on the market. She breaks a lute over a music tutor's head before she ever meets Petruchio. The play's most argued-over character: hard to read in her last scene, impossible to read in any easy way.

cast.name: Petruchio
cast.description: A young man who has come to Padua to make his fortune by marriage. He decides to marry Katherina the moment he hears about her dowry, marries her in spite of herself, and runs the second half of the play as a campaign to bring her to heel.

cast.name: Bianca
cast.description: Baptista's younger daughter, courted by everyone, presented as the model of feminine sweetness. The play allows her to be quieter than her sister and lets the last scene show her in a different light.

cast.name: Lucentio
cast.description: A young Pisan who falls in love with Bianca on sight and disguises himself as her Latin tutor to spend time with her. The romantic lead of the subplot, naive in a way Petruchio is not.

cast.name: Baptista Minola
cast.description: A wealthy Paduan gentleman, father of Katherina and Bianca. He has decided, before the play opens, that Bianca cannot marry until Katherina is settled. The whole plot moves on his refusal.

cast.name: Christopher Sly
cast.description: A drunken tinker thrown out of a tavern and picked up by a lord, who decides to play a joke on him by dressing him up as a noble and putting on a play for his amusement. The play we watch is the one performed for Sly. Shakespeare drops him after the opening scenes and never brings him back.

acclaim.quote: Petruchio is a madman in his senses; a humorist, who is not to be put out of his humour by anything that can happen.
The whole of the Taming of the Shrew is admirable. There is not a scene which is not entirely worthy of Shakespeare.

whyItMatters.title: Shakespeare's Most Uncomfortable Comedy
whyItMatters.body: The Taming of the Shrew has been in continuous production for four hundred years, and for at least three hundred of those years audiences and critics have been trying to figure out how to feel about it. The Restoration rewrote it. The Victorians cut it. Twentieth-century productions experimented with making Katherina's final speech sarcastic, or whispered, or weeping. Some directors stage it with a wink between Katherina and Petruchio that turns the speech into a private joke; some stage it straight, as a defeat; some end it with Sly being thrown back into the gutter, suggesting the whole play is the kind of male fantasy a drunk tinker would enjoy. The play is famous because it does not let an audience settle. Almost no other Shakespeare comedy is rewritten as often as Shrew, and no other Shakespeare comedy provokes the same argument across the centuries about whether it can be performed at all. That argument is part of what the play means now.

whyItMatters.title: The Lost Frame
whyItMatters.body: The Taming of the Shrew starts twice. Before Petruchio and Katherina exist, the audience meets Christopher Sly, a drunken tinker who is found asleep outside an alehouse by a hunting lord. The lord and his servants decide, for fun, to dress Sly in fine clothes, put him in a soft bed, and convince him when he wakes that he is a noble who has been mad for years. A travelling theatre company performs The Taming of the Shrew for his entertainment. Sly watches one scene, says he wishes it were over, and disappears from the text. He is never closed off; the framing device just stops. Almost every other Shakespeare frame closes — Hamlet returns to Fortinbras, A Midsummer Night's Dream ends with Puck speaking to the audience. Shrew leaves Sly hanging, and the silence has been read every way: as Shakespeare giving up on the device, as the printer losing a final scene, or as a deliberate refusal to let the audience pretend it has just been watching a story rather than the story a drunk wanted to see. The last reading is the most modern, and the most uncomfortable.

whyItMatters.title: The Final Speech
whyItMatters.body: At the end of the play, the three new husbands wager on whose wife is the most obedient. Katherina is the only one of the three who comes when she is called. Petruchio asks her to deliver a lecture to the other two wives on a wife's duty to her husband, and she does — a forty-five-line set piece about how women should place their hands beneath their husbands' feet. It is the longest speech any woman gives in any Shakespeare comedy. What to do with it is the play's whole legacy. The text itself gives the actor nothing to work against: there are no asides, no signals of irony, no breaks in the rhetoric. Productions have tried every interpretation: Mary Pickford in the 1929 film delivered the line with a giant wink at Bianca; some modern productions have Katherina speak it straight as defeat; others as a settled bargain with the husband she has, in fact, come to love. Whatever Shakespeare meant, the speech is the largest single test he ever set his audience: how do you read four hundred lines of submission when the woman delivering them is the smartest character in the play?
